steps.text: Write the "Overview" section of a Wikipedia article on the HarmonyOS App (.app) file format, explaining App Packs, HAP files and how they evolved, and the shared package types HAR and HSP.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
### App Pack and HAP files
- what an App Pack is; comparison to apk/msi/deb
- building with DevEco Studio; HAP contents and module types
- history of the HAP format (two stages)
- debugging and distribution
### Shared packages
- HAR vs HSP
- HSP restrictions; OpenHarmony 4.1 API 11 improvements

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
### App Pack and HAP files
- HarmonyOS apps distributed as software package file: App Pack / App file, suffix .app
  - analogous to apk (Android), msi (Microsoft Windows), deb package (Debian-based OSes)
- making an app: development tool e.g. DevEco Studio to code and pack HarmonyOS Ability Package (HAP) and associated files into app package
- HAP files: resources, third-party libraries, configuration files
  - two module types: entry and feature
  - entry = main module, must be in app package; feature = additional modules implementing app features
  - App file with different builds/specs optimized for various devices may contain more than one entry HAP
- history, two phases
  - first stage: after decompression, non-executable APK as program entrance, connects with AOSP file libraries of binaries; AOSP base of HarmonyOS 1.0.1 with API 5 for TVs, HarmonyOS 2.0 with API 6 for phones and tablets
  - cause: imperfect ecology of early development of new format during dual framework of OpenHarmony L3-L5 (EMUI Android base convergence)
  - third party developers facilitated mixed packaging of APK and HAP
  - second stage: HAR libraries on HarmonyOS 3.1 API 9, ArkUI declarative framework, ArkTS (evolved from eTS on 3.0) as primary language replacing Java binaries
  - APKs eliminated after decompression on HarmonyOS 3.1 Developer Preview API 9 Stage model Ability; HAP cannot be converted into APKs by simple unpacking/packaging -> HAP not a casing of APK
- before packing into App Pack: HAP files can run directly on real device or emulator for debugging/verifying
- after development: apps with signature information distributed to devices with AppGallery Connect (tool kit of services for creation, development, distribution, maintenance)
### Shared packages
- two kinds for sharing code/resources in App Pack: Harmony Archive (HAR, static), Harmony Shared Package (HSP, dynamic)
- both share code, C++ libraries, resources, configuration files
  - HAR: compiled together with invoking modules -> possibly multiple copies
  - HSP: independent compilation -> only one copy in build product
- multiple HAPs referencing same HAR -> use HSP to share some state variables, reduce App Pack size
- HSP restrictions: no declaration of abilities in its configuration file; invoking modules must be in same stage model
- OpenHarmony 4.1 API 11: System-level HSP supporting OTA upgrades in App Package Management system
  - Public Basic Class Library: creation of Workers within HSP and HAR; user gives task and continues while worker(s) (Thread pools) process task on different thread
  - call back method initiated when special method provided on initial call gets called

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
### App Pack and HAP files

HarmonyOS apps are distributed as a software package file that is called the App Pack or the App file, and it has the suffix .app. It is like other software packages such as the apk used by the Android operating system, msi in Microsoft Windows, or a deb package in Debian-based operating systems.

To make a HarmonyOS app you need a software development tool like DevEco Studio, which is used to code and pack the HarmonyOS Ability Package (HAP) and the associated files into an app package.

The HAP files can have resources, third-party libraries and configuration files in them. There are two types of modules, entry and feature. The entry type of HAP file is the main module and it has to be included in an app package, and the feature type HAP files are additional modules that implement the features of the apps. Also, an App file that has different builds and specifications optimized for the various devices can contain more than one HAP file of the entry type.

The development of the HAP format went through two phases historically. In the first stage, after decompression, there was a non-executable APK that was the program entrance, to connect with AOSP file libraries of binaries to interact with the AOSP base of HarmonyOS 1.0.1 with API 5 for TVs and HarmonyOS 2.0 with API 6 for phones and tablets. This was because of the imperfect ecology of the early development of the new app file format during the dual framework of OpenHarmony L3-L5 that consists of EMUI Android base convergence. In early app development, third party developers facilitated development for mixed packaging of APK and HAP. In the second stage of HAP, HAR libraries were introduced on HarmonyOS 3.1 API 9 with the ArkUI declarative programming framework, and ArkTS, which evolved from eTS on 3.0, became the primary programming language replacing Java binaries. APKs were eliminated after decompression on HarmonyOS 3.1 Developer Preview API 9 Stage model Ability, and HAP cannot be converted into APKs by simple unpacking and packaging, so the HAP file format is not a casing of the APK.

Before they are packed into an App Pack, HAP files can run directly on a real device or an emulator so developers can debug and verify the apps during development.

After development, apps that contain signature information can be distributed to different devices with AppGallery Connect, which is a tool kit of services for creation, development, distribution and maintenance of an app.

### Shared packages

- two kinds of shared packages for sharing code and resources in an App Pack: Harmony Archive (HAR, static) and Harmony Shared Package (HSP, dynamic)
- both share code, C++ libraries, resources, configuration files; HAR compiled with invoking modules -> maybe multiple copies; HSP compiled independently -> one copy in build product
- many HAPs referencing same HAR -> HSP instead, share some state variables, smaller App Pack
- HSP restrictions: no abilities declared in its configuration file; invoking modules in same stage model as HSP
- OpenHarmony 4.1 API 11: System-level HSP with OTA upgrades in App Package Management system; Workers within HSP and HAR (Public Basic Class Library), thread pools, task on different thread; call back method

steps.text:
### App Pack and HAP files

HarmonyOS apps are distributed as a software package file that is called the App Pack or the App file, and it has the suffix .app. It is like other software packages such as the apk used by the Android operating system, msi in Microsoft Windows, or a deb package in Debian-based operating systems.

To make a HarmonyOS app you need a software development tool like DevEco Studio, which is used to code and pack the HarmonyOS Ability Package (HAP) and the associated files into an app package.

The HAP files can have resources, third-party libraries and configuration files in them. There are two types of modules, entry and feature. The entry type of HAP file is the main module and it has to be included in an app package, and the feature type HAP files are additional modules that implement the features of the apps. Also, an App file that has different builds and specifications optimized for the various devices can contain more than one HAP file of the entry type.

The development of the HAP format went through two phases historically. In the first stage, after decompression, there was a non-executable APK that was the program entrance, to connect with AOSP file libraries of binaries to interact with the AOSP base of HarmonyOS 1.0.1 with API 5 for TVs and HarmonyOS 2.0 with API 6 for phones and tablets. This was because of the imperfect ecology of the early development of the new app file format during the dual framework of OpenHarmony L3-L5 that consists of EMUI Android base convergence. In early app development, third party developers facilitated development for mixed packaging of APK and HAP. In the second stage of HAP, HAR libraries were introduced on HarmonyOS 3.1 API 9 with the ArkUI declarative programming framework, and ArkTS, which evolved from eTS on 3.0, became the primary programming language replacing Java binaries. APKs were eliminated after decompression on HarmonyOS 3.1 Developer Preview API 9 Stage model Ability, and HAP cannot be converted into APKs by simple unpacking and packaging, so the HAP file format is not a casing of the APK.

Before they are packed into an App Pack, HAP files can run directly on a real device or an emulator so developers can debug and verify the apps during development.

After development, apps that contain signature information can be distributed to different devices with AppGallery Connect, which is a tool kit of services for creation, development, distribution and maintenance of an app.

### Shared packages

To share code and resources in an App Pack, the operating system has two kinds of shared packages. Harmony Archive (HAR) is a static shared package, and Harmony Shared Package (HSP) is a dynamic shared package.

HAR and HSP both let you share code, C++ libraries, resources, and configuration files. In HAR the code and resources get compiled together with the invoking modules, and this can result in multiple copies of the same code and resources. HSP on the other hand allows independent compilation, so there is only one copy of the code and resources in the build product.

When the same HAR is referenced by multiple HAPs, HSP can be used instead to share some state variables and to reduce the size of the App Pack. But HSP has some restrictions. For example, it does not support declaring abilities in its configuration file, and its invoking modules have to be in the same stage model as the HSP.

OpenHarmony 4.1 API 11 brought improvements with System-level HSP that supports OTA upgrades within the App Package Management system. The API 11 upgrade under the Public Basic Class Library also supports creating Workers within HSP and HAR. This is something where a user gives a task and continues in the process, while the worker, or multiple workers which are also known as Thread pools, process the task on a different thread. A call back method is initiated when a special method that was provided on the initial call gets called.

HarmonyOS apps are distributed as a software package file known as the App Pack or the App file, suffixed with .app, which is similar to other software packages such as apk used by the Android operating system, msi in Microsoft Windows, or a deb package in Debian-based operating systems.

The entry type of HAP file is the main module and must be included in an app package, while the feature type of HAP file is an additional module for implementing the features of the apps.

Moreover, an App file that contains different builds and specifications optimized for the various devices may contain more than one HAP file of the entry type.[2]

Historically, the development of the HAP format has gone through two phases. In the first stage, after decompression, there was a non-executable APK as the program entrance to connect with AOSP file libraries of binaries to interact with the AOSP base of HarmonyOS 1.0.1 with API 5 for TVs and HarmonyOS 2.0 with API 6 for phones and tablets, which was caused by the imperfect ecology of the early development of the new app file format during the dual framework of OpenHarmony L3-L5 that consists of EMUI Android base convergence. ### Shared packages

For sharing code and resources in an App Pack, the operating system offers two kinds of shared packages: Harmony Archive (HAR), a static shared package, and Harmony Shared Package (HSP), a dynamic shared package.[6]

Both HAR and HSP enable sharing of code, C++ libraries, resources, and configuration files.
